title: September's Global Immigration Shifts: What Changed for Visa Seekers Worldwide
excerpt: From Australia's new skilled-visa priority rules to Japan's twentyfold permanent residence fee hike and a UK settlement overhaul on the horizon, September brought rule changes that directly affect Indian migrants.
body:
• Australia overhauled skilled-visa processing on September 19 (Ministerial Directions 121 and 122): occupations in healthcare, teaching, construction, agriculture, aquaculture, fishing, resources, and defense move to the front of the queue, and applicants already in Australia now outrank offshore applicants.
  • Canada brought the UK-Canada CPTPP deal into force on September 1; from September 4, work-permit holders may study programs of six months or less without a separate study permit; Hong Kong's special PR pathways closed to new applications August 31.
  • Japan raised permanent-residence application fees from ¥10,000 to ¥200,000 — a twentyfold jump — effective October 1, with change-of-status and extension fees now scaled to the length of stay granted (¥10,000 to ¥75,000).
  • What it means for you: Indian graduates in Australia applying for PR from onshore (subclasses 189, 190, 491) get a processing edge over applicants filing from India; anyone nearing five years in the UK should watch the expected earned-settlement announcement before year-end; New Zealand visitor and transit visas are now online-only — paper applications ended October 1.

Opening lead

September brought a wave of immigration rule changes across major destination countries, from Australia's new skilled-visa priority system to Japan's twentyfold permanent-residence fee hike. Compiled in WR Immigration's September global recap, they directly affect work authorization, study rights, and processing order for millions of migrants — including large Indian communities in Canada, Australia, and the UK.

Context & Background

Most of September's changes were regulatory refinements rather than new laws. Australia replaced its skilled-visa processing order barely two months after issuing the previous one; the UK moves follow months of debate over right-to-work enforcement and a promised shift to "earned settlement"; Japan's fee increases take effect October 1.

Impact & Analysis

Australia: Ministerial Directions 121 and 122, introduced September 19, set a new priority processing order for skilled visas. Top priority goes to subclass 482 and legacy TSS applicants nominated in healthcare, teaching, construction, agriculture, aquaculture, fishing, resources, and defense and law enforcement — provided the role itself directly supports the industry. The same sectors top the queue for permanent and provisional skilled visas (subclasses 186, 187, 189, 190, 191, 489, 491, 494, 887, and 888). The most notable shift: applicants physically in Australia when they lodge now clearly outrank comparable offshore applicants. The directions change processing order only, not eligibility, and guarantee no timeframe.

Separately, Australia will attach Condition 8503 ("No Further Stay") to all subclass 600 visitor visas issued under the Approved Destination and Sponsored Family streams — blocking onshore partner-visa applications from those streams — and may apply it to Tourist and Business stream visas at the department's discretion.

Canada: The UK's accession to the CPTPP took effect between Canada and the UK on September 1, opening a new work-authorization framework for eligible UK nationals. From September 4, a temporary public policy lets work-permit holders study programs of six months or less without a separate study permit. Service Canada also clarified, effective September 18, how it determines the true employer in LMIA applications. And Canada's special permanent-residence pathways for Hong Kong residents closed to new applications on August 31.

United Kingdom: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told the Home Affairs Committee on September 15 that the proposed earned-settlement model would assess contributions and integration rather than mere five-year residence, with a formal announcement expected before year-end. Updated right-to-work guidance applies to contracts entered from October 1, extending employer liability to worker contracts, individual subcontractors, and online matching services, with civil penalties of up to £60,000 per illegal worker.

Japan: Permanent-residence fees jumped from ¥10,000 to ¥200,000 for applications from October 1; change and extension fees now range from ¥10,000 to ¥75,000 depending on the length of stay granted.

Elsewhere: Saudi Arabia set work-visa quotas for newly established businesses — two visas initially under the Establishing Programme, up to five for firms under two years old, up to 50 beyond that. New Zealand moved visitor and transit applications online-only from October 1, ending paper filings. Thailand opened automated immigration e-gates at Bangkok airport.

Diaspora Angle

Indians are among the largest migrant groups in Canada, Australia, and the UK. Australia's onshore-first processing is a tailwind for Indian students and graduates already in the country seeking permanent residence — and a relative headwind for skilled workers applying from India. In the UK, the looming earned-settlement model is the one to watch: thousands of Indians on Skilled Worker visas are approaching the five-year mark, and a shift from residence-based to contribution-based settlement could change who qualifies and when. Canada's new study flexibility helps Indian work-permit holders add short courses without fresh paperwork.

What's Next

The UK's formal earned-settlement announcement, expected before year-end, is the single most consequential item on this list for Indian migrants. Applicants and employers should also watch how Australia applies the new priority-evidence requirements in practice.
